title: Akira
summary: Akira is a ransomware operation that public reporting tracks from early 2023 onward, and its defining feature is double extortion: steal data first, then encrypt, then threaten publication. Reporting describes initial access through virtual private network services that lack multi-factor authentication, using credentials that appear to have been harvested elsewhere and reused. The operation maintains separate encryptors for Windows and for Linux hosts, including virtualisation servers, which lets it damage the backup and virtual machine infrastructure many organisations depend on for recovery. Investigators see the pattern in authentication logs from edge appliances, in the creation of new local accounts, and in bulk file rename events on shared storage. Attribution is contested: several vendors report links to earlier ransomware crews, but that judgement varies in confidence between reports, and the name has also been used for an unrelated older malware family, which causes confusion in older references.

beginner.definition: Akira is the name of a ransomware operation, a criminal business that steals data and then locks files. The attackers ask for payment to unlock the files and to stop them publishing the stolen data. Public reports show the group often enters through remote access services. It attacks both Windows computers and Linux servers.
beginner.whyItMatters: Losing your files is painful, but losing your secrets is worse. Akira steals data first, so paying for the unlock does not undo the theft. If your remote access service has no second check, such as a code on your phone, it is an easy target. Backups help only when the attackers cannot reach them too.
howItWorks: The criminals buy or find stolen usernames and passwords for a company's remote access service.
If that service asks only for a password, they can log in and look like an employee.
They explore the network, copy important files, and keep those copies outside the company.
They create new accounts so they can return even if the stolen password is changed.
Then they run a program that scrambles files on computers and on backup servers.
Finally they leave a note that demands payment and threatens to publish the stolen data.
beginner.example: Imagine a rented storage unit with a keypad lock. The code is a simple number that many people know and never change. A thief learns the code and visits at night for several weeks. He photographs the boxes and copies important papers. Then one night he fills the locks with glue and leaves a note asking for money to remove it. Changing the code now does not help, because he copied the keys long ago and already holds your documents.
takeaways: Add a second check to every remote login, not only a password.
Keep at least one backup that the main network cannot delete or change.
Watch for new accounts and sudden bulk file renames, because they signal an attack.

objectives: Explain what double extortion means and why it changes recovery priorities.
Describe how stolen credentials against a remote access service become initial access.
Identify the log and file system evidence that a ransomware intrusion leaves behind.
Explain why encryptors aimed at virtualisation and backup hosts are especially damaging.
Summarise the backup design properties that make recovery possible without paying.
Describe how contested attribution affects the wording of a threat report.
